query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the particle velocity during the HVAF-i7 torch spraying process will overcome the thickness limitation of FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coats.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a size range of 15-45 μm
generation.intervention: Increasing the particle velocity during the HVAF-i7 torch spraying process
generation.conditions: HVAF-i7 torch spraying process, internal diameters as small as 120 mm
generation.structural_mediator: In-flight oxidation and phase transformations of the powder
generation.mechanism: The increased particle velocity will enhance the deposition efficiency and promote the formation of a dense and adherent coating, leading to improved thickness and coating integrity
generation.predicted_outcome: A sufficiently thick and adherent bond coat with minimal as-sprayed oxidation and improved durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service
generation.baseline: 15-45 μm feedstock baseline with inadequate thickness
generation.boundary: Internal diameters as small as 120 mm
generation.uncertainty: The optimal particle velocity and spray distance for the HVAF-i7 torch spraying process are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with varying particle velocities and spray distances
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating thickness does not increase with increasing particle velocity, or if the deposition efficiency and oxidation behavior do not improve, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: As reported in [,,,], HVOF as-sprayed AlTiCrFeCoNi coatings possessed a dense microstructure and a high microhardness over 750 HV with a good fracture toughness. The heat-treated NiCoFeCrSiAlTi coating exhibits a hardness even higher than 800 HV, good wear resistance, and oxidation resistance at 1100 °C, similar to that of MCrAlY coating []. The cavitation erosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi coating is about 3.5 times that of 06Cr13Ni5Mo steel in the same environment []. The high wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA at elevated temperatures is associated with oxidation behavior. The formation of a compact oxide layer on the AlCoCrFeNi and AlTiCrFeCoNi HVOF coatings accounts for enhanced wear resistance at temperatures ≥ 800 °C [] and a lowered coefficient of friction due to its function as a solid lubricant []. In [], it was found that additions of Nd and Mo to a AlCrFeCoNi base significantly reduced the wear depth at increasing temperatures due to improved oxide layer adhesion. Thus, AlCoCrFeNiMo coatings deposited using HVOF are suitable for high-temperature application. A unique feature of thermal spray processes is the extremely high heating and cooling rates (>106 K/s) [,,

Thus, in-flight oxidation of the AlCoCrFeNi particle during the spraying process can be beneficial for the tribological performance of the HEA coatings. Due to high specific surface area, the powder can oxidize differently from the cast bulk alloy. Moreover, the formation of multiple oxides—alumina, chromia, and spinel—changes the residual particle’s core composition and can lead to phase destabilization. Therefore, understanding the regularity of the oxidation behavior and phase transformation of the high-entropy powder at different conditions should be necessary for the production of a coating with high and determined property levels. In this work, the oxidation behavior and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder, produced via gas atomization, were studied. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and under prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 HVOF coatings were produced using various distances from the spray nozzle to the substrate to produce coatings with different oxide contents, and the coatings’ properties were investigated.

The topic of high-entropy alloys was investigated by a couple of studies during the past decade. The possibility of composition designing according to a targeted application was an appealing property of these types of alloys [,,]. The studies were conducted on different compositions, mechanical properties, thermal resistance and microstructures [,,]. The corrosion and erosion resistance of CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coatings manufactured by laser metal deposition technique was previously tested in a geothermal environment []. The results revealed good erosion resistance and no corrosion damage when exposed to different conditions, leading to the conclusion that this type of newly developed coating is suitable for aggressive media Zihui Dong et al. [] studied CoCrFeMo0/85Ni powder, produced by atomization, for differential thermal analyses and differential scanning calorimetry to assess the thermodynamic properties including solidus, liquidus and phase transitions temperatures. Their study revealed that the complex FCC matrix of the high-entropy alloy was embedded with multiple phases which are the mixture of the Co-, Cr-, Fe-rich tetragonal phase and Mo-rich rhombohedral phases.
